properties.name: Bovillae
properties.notes: Bovillae stood 11 Roman miles from Rome on the Via Appia and was the first major stop travelers reached leaving the city. It was an old Latin League town and the seat of a cult the Julian family kept up because they claimed descent from its Alban founders.

properties.name: Aricia
properties.notes: Aricia sat at the 16th milestone of the Via Appia below the Alban Hills and marked the end of the road's first climb out of Rome. The town held the famous grove and lake sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis nearby and was a well-known overnight halt for travelers.

properties.name: Tres Tabernae
properties.notes: Tres Tabernae, Three Taverns, sat 33 miles from Rome where the Via Appia met the branch road running up from Antium. The Book of Acts records that believers from Rome walked out to meet Paul here as he traveled to the city under guard.

properties.name: Forum Appii
properties.notes: Forum Appii stood 43 miles from Rome at the head of a canal that ran alongside the road through the Pontine Marshes. Horace described it as crowded with bargemen and overpriced innkeepers when he stopped there on his journey to Brundisium in 37 BCE.

properties.name: Terracina
properties.notes: Tarracina, called Anxur by the Volscians who built it, occupied a limestone bluff overlooking the point where the Via Appia rejoined the coast after the Pontine Marshes crossing. A temple to Jupiter Anxur crowned the height above the town and the harbor, later improved under Trajan, served coastal traffic.

properties.name: Fundi
properties.notes: Fundi sat on a shelf of the Via Appia above the Fondi plain, sixteen miles beyond Tarracina by the itinerary's count. Horace and Martial both mention it as a stop on the road south, and the town later supplied its own line of Roman consuls.

properties.name: Formiae
properties.notes: Formiae lay on the Gulf of Gaeta and served travelers on the Via Appia as well as wealthy Romans who built villas along its shore. Cicero owned a villa here and was murdered nearby in 43 BCE while trying to flee by sea.

properties.name: Minturnae
properties.notes: Minturnae stood where the Via Appia crossed the Liris river on a bridge just above the ancient port, and Rome planted a citizen colony there in 296 BCE to hold the crossing. The forum, theater, and baths uncovered at the site show a substantial road town rather than a simple waystop.

properties.name: Sinuessa
properties.notes: Sinuessa marked the point where the Via Appia left the Tyrrhenian coast for good and turned inland toward Capua. Its inn, the Tabernae Caediciae, was well known enough that Horace mentioned staying there, and the town's warm sulfur springs drew visitors on top of road traffic.

properties.name: Pons Campanus
properties.notes: Pons Campanus carried the Via Appia over the Savone stream on the stretch between Sinuessa and Casilinum. No excavated remains have been tied to it with certainty, so this point is placed by interpolating along the known road corridor between its two identified neighbors.

properties.name: Ad Octavum
properties.notes: Ad Octavum took its name from standing at the eighth Roman milestone out of Capua on the Via Appia toward Sinuessa. Its exact spot has not been pinned down archaeologically, so it is placed here by that mile-marker distance along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Casilinum
properties.notes: Casilinum sat three miles northwest of Capua where the Via Appia crossed the Volturnus river and met the Via Latina coming down from the north. Hannibal besieged the town in 216 BCE and its garrison held out on a starvation diet until Roman relief broke through the following year.

properties.name: Calatia
properties.notes: Calatia stood six miles southeast of Capua on the Via Appia at the point where the road to Beneventum bent east toward the mountains. Its history ran alongside Capua's own and it lost its independent status once Rome brought the region firmly under control.

properties.name: Caudium
properties.notes: Caudium controlled the narrow pass of the Caudine Forks, where a Roman army was trapped and forced under the yoke by the Samnites in 321 BCE. By the imperial period it was a regular mansio on the Via Appia, 21 miles from Capua and 11 from Beneventum.

properties.name: Ad Calorem
properties.notes: Ad Calorem stood where the Via Appia crossed the Calore river ten miles out of Beneventum on the way to Aeclanum, at a bridge later called Ponte Appiano. No confirmed find marks the station itself, so it is placed here along the known road corridor at its recorded mile distance.

properties.name: Aeclanum
properties.notes: Aeclanum was the chief town of the Hirpini and stood 15 miles from Beneventum on the Via Appia's route toward Venusia and Tarentum. The emperor Trajan had the stretch of road between the two towns repaired, and the site today is an open archaeological park at Passo di Mirabella.

properties.name: Sub Romula
properties.notes: Sub Romula was the next stage on the Via Appia after Aeclanum, 21 miles along the road toward the Ofanto crossing and Venusia. Scholars place it at modern Lacedonia, identified in Pleiades as ancient Aquilonia, on the Samnite border in the hill country east of Aeclanum.

properties.name: Pons Aufidi
properties.notes: Pons Aufidi carried the Via Appia over the Aufidus river, today's Ofanto, on the last stretch before Venusia. Both the Peutinger Table and the Antonine Itinerary record the crossing, and it has traditionally been identified with the bridge known as Ponte San Venere, though some recent surveys favor a Roman bridge further south instead.

properties.name: Venusia
properties.notes: Venusia became a Latin colony in 291 BCE after Rome's victory in the Third Samnite War and grew into a major stop on the Via Appia, 77 miles out of Beneventum by the itinerary's count. The poet Horace was born there in 65 BCE, the son of a freedman auctioneer.

properties.name: Silvium
properties.notes: Silvium was the first stage the Via Appia reached after Venusia on the direct route toward Tarentum, sited on the high ground near modern Gravina in Puglia. Recent fieldwork by Luciano Piepoli has proposed pinning the station more precisely to the Santo Staso area just outside Gravina rather than the older Botromagno identification.

properties.name: Blera
properties.notes: Blera was a station on the Apulian stretch of the Via Appia, 13 miles beyond Silvium on the way to Tarentum. Its site has not been securely fixed on the ground, though Luciano Piepoli's fieldwork has proposed the masseria Castello locality as a candidate, so this point is interpolated along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Sub Lupatia
properties.notes: Sub Lupatia followed Blera on the Via Appia's Apulian stretch, 14 miles further toward Tarentum. Luciano Piepoli's fieldwork has proposed the masseria Caione locality as its site, but without a secure identification this point is interpolated along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Canales
properties.notes: Canales was the last named stage of the Via Appia before Tarentum, 13 miles beyond Sub Lupatia. Its exact site remains unfixed, so this point is interpolated along the known road corridor between Sub Lupatia and Tarentum.

properties.name: Tarentum
properties.notes: Tarentum was the great Greek colony of Magna Graecia on the gulf that bore its name, and the Via Appia reached it 157 miles out of Beneventum by the itinerary's reckoning. From here the road turned east across the heel of Italy toward Brundisium.

properties.name: Uria
properties.notes: Uria, modern Oria, was a Messapian town the Via Appia passed through on its way from Tarentum to Brundisium, a stretch the itinerary gives as 44 miles in total. The split of that total between Tarentum and Uria is estimated here from the towns' known positions, since the itinerary records only the combined figure.

properties.name: Brundisium
properties.notes: Brundisium was the Via Appia's terminus and Rome's principal naval harbor on the Adriatic, reached from Tarentum by 44 miles of road according to the itinerary. Its double-armed natural harbor made it the standard crossing point to Greece and the eastern provinces, and Horace's own journey along this road, described in his Satires, ended here.

properties.name: Dyrrachium
properties.notes: Dyrrachium, modern Durrës, was the Adriatic terminus of the Via Egnatia and the main port linking Italy to the Balkans; travelers from Brundisium landed here to start the overland road east. The Romans took the city (originally the Greek colony Epidamnos) under their protection in 229 BCE and it grew into a major military and commercial hub of Illyricum.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: This Apollonia in Illyria was the road's second Adriatic starting point, a short march south of Dyrrachium, and its branch of the Via Egnatia joined the main line at Ad Quintum. The city was a renowned center of learning where the young Octavian was studying under Athenodorus when news of Caesar's assassination reached him in 44 BCE.

properties.name: Ad Quintum
properties.notes: Ad Quintum, at the fifth milestone out of Dyrrachium, was the point where the Dyrrachium and Apollonia branches of the Via Egnatia physically merged into a single road. The site is identified with Bradashesh near Elbasan, where excavations have uncovered a Roman villa and a well-preserved bathhouse dated to the mid-2nd century CE.
sources: Not in Itin. Ant. station list; attested via milestone toponym

properties.name: Clodiana
properties.notes: Clodiana was a horse-changing station on the Shkumbin river valley stretch of the road, now identified with modern Peqin in central Albania. A Roman-period castle foundation still stands on the site, and the station appears by name in both the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table.

properties.name: Scampis
properties.notes: Scampis (Mansio Scampa) sat on the Shkumbin river at the site of modern Elbasan and grew from a Roman trading post into a walled city with towers by the 3rd or 4th century CE. It appears under this name in the Antonine Itinerary and as Scampis or Hiscampis in the Peutinger Table and the Bordeaux pilgrim's account.

properties.name: Tres Tabernae
properties.notes: This Tres Tabernae (a different place from the better-known station of the same name on the Via Appia) was the horse-changing post where the road began climbing out of the Shkumbin valley toward the Candavian mountains. It is identified with modern Qukës in Albania, where sections of the original paved road survive nearby.

properties.name: Lychnidus
properties.notes: Lychnidus, today's Ohrid, stood on the shore of the lake that still bears a version of its name and was the chief town of the mountain crossing between Illyricum and Macedonia. It later gave its name to the medieval and modern city, one of the longest continuously inhabited settlements on the whole road.

properties.name: Nicaea
properties.notes: This Macedonian Nicaea (not the famous Nicaea in Bithynia) is named in the Antonine Itinerary between Lychnidus and Heraclea Lyncestis, but scholars disagree on its exact site, with the Resen basin and the Bukovo pass area the leading candidates. The coordinate given here is a rough placement near Resen, North Macedonia, along the attested road corridor rather than a confirmed excavation.

properties.name: Heraclea Lyncestis
properties.notes: Heraclea Lyncestis, founded by Philip II of Macedon and now an excavated site on the edge of Bitola, was the major crossroads town where the Via Egnatia met the road running south to Thessaly. Its well-preserved Roman theater and later Early Christian basilicas with mosaic floors are still visible on site today.

properties.name: Cellae
properties.notes: Cellae marked the road's passage around Lake Ostrovo (modern Lake Vegoritida) on its way toward Edessa, and its precise site has been argued over since Charles Edson's 1951 study fixed the general area near Arnissa. The coordinate here sits at Arnissa as the best-supported approximate location rather than a firmly excavated find-spot.
sources: Edson, "The Location of Cellae and the Route of the Via Egnatia," Classical Philology 46 (1951)

properties.name: Edessa
properties.notes: Edessa, called Vodena for much of its later history, sits on a bluff over a dramatic set of waterfalls and controlled the western approach to the Macedonian plain.

properties.name: Pella
properties.notes: Pella was the birthplace of Alexander the Great and had served as the royal capital of Macedon before Rome absorbed the kingdom in 168 BCE. By 117 CE it was a Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, and its excavated House of Dionysos preserves some of the finest surviving pebble mosaics from the Hellenistic world.

properties.name: Thessalonica
properties.notes: Thessalonica was the provincial capital of Macedonia and the largest city the Via Egnatia passed through, straddling the road at the head of the Thermaic Gulf. Paul the Apostle preached in its synagogue on his journey along this same road, and the modern city's main street, Egnatia Street, still traces the ancient route.

properties.name: Melissourgis
properties.notes: Melissourgis was a station east of Thessalonica on the road skirting the lakes of Koroneia and Volvi, and its name plausibly survives in the modern village of Melissourgos in the Volvi municipality. The identification rests on toponymic continuity rather than confirmed archaeological remains, so the coordinate is an approximation.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: This second Apollonia on the route, distinct from the Adriatic city of the same name, stood on the southern shore of Lake Volvi in the district of Mygdonia. Settlers from Chalkidiki founded it around 432 BCE; Philip II later destroyed it before Rome resettled the site.

properties.name: Amphipolis
properties.notes: Amphipolis commanded the crossing of the Strymon river and had been fought over since classical times, most famously in the battle where the Athenian general Cleon and the Spartan Brasidas both died in 422 BCE. Its ruins, including a well-preserved Roman bridge foundation and the nearby Kasta Tomb, lie by the modern village of Amfipoli.

properties.name: Philippi
properties.notes: Philippi, founded by and named for Philip II of Macedon, became a Roman veteran colony after Octavian and Mark Antony crushed the assassins of Caesar just outside its walls in 42 BCE. Paul the Apostle later established the first Christian church on European soil here, and the site's forum, theater, and basilicas are exceptionally well preserved.

properties.name: Neapolis
properties.notes: Neapolis was the Aegean port that served Philippi and the point where sea travelers from Troas, including Paul the Apostle, first stepped onto the Via Egnatia. The city sat on the peninsula now occupied by Kavala, whose old town still overlaps much of the ancient site.

properties.name: Acontisma
properties.notes: Acontisma was a fortified guard post on a hill east of Neapolis that controlled a narrow pass on the frontier between Macedonia and Thrace. Its walls, first built in the 4th century BCE and reused for centuries after, sit about two miles east of the modern town of Nea Karvali.

properties.name: Topeiros
properties.notes: Topeiros began as a Via Egnatia way station and was rebuilt as a proper Greek-style city under Trajan around the turn of the 2nd century CE, taking the name Ulpia Topirus. Its ruins lie between the villages of Toxotes and Paradeisos west of Xanthi, near the crossing of the Nestos river.

properties.name: Cosintos
properties.notes: Cosintos is named in the Antonine Itinerary between Topeiros and Porsulae and almost certainly marks the road's crossing of the Kosynthos river near Xanthi, but no excavated station has been firmly tied to the name. The coordinate given is an estimate along the road corridor between its two better-identified neighbors.

properties.name: Porsulae
properties.notes: Porsulae was a Thracian civitas on the Via Egnatia that later grew into the better-known Byzantine city of Maximianopolis (also called Mosynopolis), sited about seven kilometers west of modern Komotini. In 117 CE it was still known by its older name, Porsulae, recorded in the Antonine Itinerary.

properties.name: Brendice
properties.notes: Brendice is known only from its listing in the Antonine Itinerary between Porsulae and Milolitum, and no modern site has been securely matched to it. Its coordinate here is a rough interpolation along the attested road path between its two neighboring stations, not a confirmed find-spot.

properties.name: Milolitum
properties.notes: Milolitum appears in the Antonine Itinerary as a minor stop between Brendice and Tempyra in eastern Thrace, but like its neighbors it has no confirmed modern identification. The coordinate given is an estimate along the known road corridor rather than an excavated location.

properties.name: Tempyra
properties.notes: Tempyra was the last stop before Traianopolis, sitting just west of the Evros/Hebros river in the area around modern Feres. Its distance to Traianopolis, nine Roman miles, is independently confirmed by two ancient sources that agree exactly on the figure.

properties.name: Traianopolis
properties.notes: Traianopolis was founded by the emperor Trajan on the site of the ancient town of Doriscus, where Xerxes had once mustered his invasion force before marching on Greece. The new city, built directly astride the Via Egnatia, is now the archaeological site of Loutra Traianoupolis near Alexandroupoli.

properties.name: Kypsela
properties.notes: Kypsela stood on the Hebros (Evros) river and was already an old, well-known town by the time Strabo wrote about it, controlling the river crossing on the road into deep Thrace. It survives today as the Turkish town of İpsala, still sitting by the same river on the modern Greek-Turkish border.

properties.name: Syracella
properties.notes: Syracella is recorded in the Antonine Itinerary as a horse-changing stop between Kypsela and Apri, but no modern site has been confidently matched to it. Its coordinate is an interpolation along the road path between its two firmly identified neighbors rather than an excavated location.

properties.name: Apri
properties.notes: Apri (Aprus) was refounded as Colonia Claudia Aprensis under Claudius as a settlement for retired Roman soldiers and became a full city on the Via Egnatia in the province of Europa. Its remains lie near the modern Turkish village of Kermeyan in Tekirdağ Province.

properties.name: Resistum
properties.notes: Resistum is attested in both Pliny the Elder and the Antonine Itinerary as lying inland from Apri on the road toward Perinthus, with Pliny giving the distance between the two as twenty-two Roman miles. No modern excavation has been tied to the name, so its coordinate is a rough placement along the road corridor.

properties.name: Perinthus
properties.notes: Perinthus was one of the great cities of ancient Thrace, a flourishing Samian and Megarian colony on the Sea of Marmara that later became a key communications hub on the Via Egnatia. In 117 CE it still carried its original name; the city was only renamed Heraclea in honor of its legendary founder around the year 300.

properties.name: Selymbria
properties.notes: Selymbria owed its importance to its natural harbor on the Sea of Marmara and its position on the coastal road toward Byzantium, twenty-two Roman miles east of Perinthus. The site is now the Turkish town of Silivri, where an open-air museum displays finds that include original Via Egnatia milestones.

properties.name: Athyras
properties.notes: Athyras was a small Thracian coastal settlement on the road between Selymbria and Byzantium, taking its name from the river that reached the sea nearby. It survives as the Istanbul district of Büyükçekmece; the distance given here is estimated from the known total of forty-four Roman miles between Selymbria and Byzantium rather than quoted directly from a surviving itinerary.
sources: Geographic distance estimated from Selymbria-Byzantium total (44 m.p.)

properties.name: Rhegion
properties.notes: Rhegion was the last staging point before Byzantium, a coastal settlement now underlying the Istanbul district of Küçükçekmece around the mouth of its namesake lake. Like the preceding leg, its distance here is estimated from the attested Selymbria-Byzantium total rather than drawn from a directly quoted itinerary figure.
sources: Geographic distance estimated from Selymbria-Byzantium total (44 m.p.)

properties.name: Byzantium
properties.notes: Byzantium was the eastern terminus of the Via Egnatia, an old Megarian colony commanding the Bosphorus strait between Europe and Asia. In 117 CE it was still an important but unremarkable provincial city of Thrace, two centuries away from Constantine's decision to remake it as his new capital.

properties.name: Segusio
properties.notes: Segusio, modern Susa, was the capital of the client kingdom of the Cottian Alps under King Cottius, who ceded it to Rome without a fight and was left ruling it as a Roman prefect. Cottius's own triumphal arch, dedicated to Augustus around 9 BCE, still stands here — one of the best-preserved Augustan monuments anywhere in the empire.
sources: Itin. Ant. 341 (Item a Mediolano per Alpes Cottias)

properties.name: Ad Martis
properties.notes: Ad Martis, modern Oulx, sat at the foot of the Montgenevre pass and took its name from a temple to Mars raised here, tradition says, to mark a victory over the Cottian dynasty before its peaceful annexation. A small fort (castrum) guarded the station in the later empire.

properties.name: Brigantio
properties.notes: Brigantio, modern Briancon, was the highest station of consequence on the Cottian Alps crossing, guarding the approach to the Montgenevre pass into Italy. Its Celtic name, shared with several other Alpine and British sites, simply means high place.

properties.name: Ramae
properties.notes: Ramae is named in the Antonine Itinerary's Cottian Alps stage between Brigantio and Eburodunum, but no excavated site has been securely matched to it. Placed here by interpolation along the Durance valley road at the recorded distance; the true location may be a few kilometers off.

properties.name: Eburodunum
properties.notes: Eburodunum, modern Embrun, guarded the Durance river crossing on the road down from the Cottian Alps into Gaul proper. Its Celtic name (yew-fort) points to an earlier Gallic hillfort on the same commanding site above the river.

properties.name: Caturrigas
properties.notes: Caturrigas, modern Chorges, gave its name to the Caturiges tribe whose territory it anchored, on the road linking the Cottian Alps crossing to Vapincum. Excavated remains include a substantial Roman-era settlement beside the modern town.

properties.name: Vapincum
properties.notes: Vapincum, modern Gap, was the junction where the Alpine road down from Italy met the true Via Domitia running west to Narbo and the Pyrenees. A civitas of the Vocontii tribal confederation, it stayed a modest town through the Roman period, not formally a colonia until far later.

properties.name: Segustero
properties.notes: Segustero, modern Sisteron, commanded the narrow gorge where the Durance cuts through the last Alpine foothills, the single easiest defensive choke point on the whole road between Vapincum and the Rhone valley. The medieval citadel above the town still marks the same strategic spot.
sources: Antonine Itinerary (Cottian Alps stage, Gallia section)

properties.name: Alabontia
properties.notes: Alabontia was the busiest crossroads station between Segustero and Apta Julia, where the Via Domitia met a north-south road into the Alpine interior. Its remains lie beneath the chapel of Notre-Dame-des-Anges near the village of Lurs, overlooking the Durance.
sources: Antonine Itinerary (Cottian Alps stage, Gallia section)

properties.name: Catuiacia
properties.notes: Catuiacia, identified with modern Céreste, was a minor relay station on the stretch of the Via Domitia climbing out of the Durance valley toward Apta Julia. Roman-period remains have been recorded in and around the village.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Item a Mediolano per Alpes Cottias)

properties.name: Apta Julia
properties.notes: Apta Julia, modern Apt, was founded as a Roman colony under Julius Caesar beside the existing road, its forum and theatre serving the fertile Calavon valley. A 1st-century CE bridge over the Calavon still stands just outside the modern town.

properties.name: Cabellio
properties.notes: Cabellio, modern Cavaillon, sat on the Durance where the Via Domitia crossed toward the Rhone, a Latin-rights town since Caesar's day with its own mint striking bronze coinage. A well-preserved Roman arch still stands in the old town.

properties.name: Ambrussum
properties.notes: Ambrussum, on the Vidourle river between Nemausus and Sextantio, is one of the best-excavated Via Domitia stations anywhere on the road — its Pont Ambroix bridge, paved street with cart ruts worn a foot deep, and roadside way-station foundations are all still visible. Distance given is the itinerary's own figure measured from Nemausus, itself some 30 Roman miles past Cabellio via the road's Rhone crossing near Arelate.

properties.name: Sextantio
properties.notes: Sextantio, at modern Castelnau-le-Lez across the Lez river from Montpellier, took its name from its position at the sixth Roman mile of a local distance count. It became the region's chief town in late antiquity, before medieval Montpellier eclipsed it.

properties.name: Forum Domitii
properties.notes: Forum Domitii, near modern Montbazin, was a market town founded alongside the road itself and named for its builder, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus — the clearest surviving trace of the man the whole route is named after.

properties.name: Cessero
properties.notes: Cessero, modern Saint-Thibery, controlled the Via Domitia's crossing of the Herault river, with a bridge whose Roman piers still support the modern span. Excavated town remains include a forum and baths.

properties.name: Baeterrae
properties.notes: Baeterrae, modern Beziers, was settled as a colony for veterans of Caesar's Seventh Legion around 36 BCE, its name recalled in the legion's own numbering on surviving inscriptions. The Pont Vieux bridge crosses the Orb on Roman foundations.

properties.name: Narbo
properties.notes: Narbo Martius, modern Narbonne, was Rome's first colony outside Italy, founded in 118 BCE the same year Domitius Ahenobarbus built this road, and it grew into the capital of Gallia Narbonensis. Its harbor on a Mediterranean lagoon made it one of the busiest ports in the western empire.

properties.name: Combusta
properties.notes: Combusta, near modern Salses-le-Chateau, marked the point where the Via Domitia entered the narrow coastal corridor between the Corbieres hills and the Etang de Salses lagoon on the final approach to Ruscino.

properties.name: Ruscino
properties.notes: Ruscino, at Chateau-Roussillon near modern Perpignan, was capital of the Roussillon region and gave that region its name. Excavations have uncovered its forum and a large public building, part of it now displayed under a protective shelter.

properties.name: Ad Centenarium
properties.notes: Ad Centenarium, near modern Le Boulou, sat on the last stretch of flat ground before the Via Domitia began its climb into the Pyrenees toward the Panissars pass and the border with Hispania.

properties.name: Summum Pyrenaeum
properties.notes: Summum Pyrenaeum, at the Col de Panissars, marked the exact boundary between Gallia Narbonensis and Hispania Tarraconensis and the end of this stage of the Via Domitia, where it continued south as the Via Augusta. Pompey raised a monumental trophy here in 71 BCE to mark his Spanish campaigns; its foundations were rediscovered in the 1980s.

properties.name: Iuncaria
properties.notes: First mansio south of Summus Pyrenaeus, controlling the Empordà plain approach into Hispania.

properties.name: Cinniana
properties.notes: Poorly localized station between Iuncaria and the Barcino road; the Vicarello cups give a different (12 mp) figure, showing source disagreement even in antiquity.

properties.name: Aquae Voconiae
properties.notes: A thermal-spring station ("Waters of Voconius"); Roman baths have been excavated at Caldes de Malavella, matching the name directly.

properties.name: Seterrae
properties.notes: Minor station on the corridor between Girona and the Vallès.

properties.name: Praetorium
properties.notes: Marks the road's entry into the Vallès plain north of Barcino.

properties.name: Semproniana
properties.notes: Named station on the Vallès stretch; some scholars treat this as an alternate/interior branch rather than the main line.

properties.name: Arrago
properties.notes: Attested name near modern Sabadell; exact placement and route order is disputed.

properties.name: Barcino
properties.notes: Colonia Iulia Augusta Faventia Paterna Barcino, founded c. 15-13 BCE; a major node where the Via Augusta met the port.

properties.name: Ad Fines
properties.notes: A boundary-marker station ("at the border") at the Llobregat river crossing, the traditional edge of Barcino's territory.

properties.name: Antistiana
properties.notes: Sits on the Penedès stretch, bypassing the impassable Garraf coastal cliffs.

properties.name: Stabulum Novum
properties.notes: Attested name meaning "new stable/inn"; no firm archaeological fix, placed on the Baix Penedès corridor.

properties.name: Palfuriana
properties.notes: Precisely located per the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire, at the coastal approach to Tarraco.

properties.name: Tarraco
properties.notes: Capital of Hispania Tarraconensis and the road's major hub; extensive Roman remains now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

properties.name: Oleastrum
properties.notes: Sits at the mountain pass ("Sub Saltu," below the pass) where the road crosses from the Camp de Tarragona into the Ebro corridor.

properties.name: Traiecta
properties.notes: Name suggests a river or lagoon crossing point in the Ebro delta; exact site not fixed.

properties.name: Dertosa
properties.notes: Major Ebro-crossing city and conventus-level town; the road's bridge/ferry point over the river.

properties.name: Intibili
properties.notes: Approximately placed on the coastal-inland stretch through the Baix Maestrat; no firm modern town identification.

properties.name: Ildum
properties.notes: Well-studied mansio, cited also on the Vicarello cups and in the Ravenna Cosmography.
sources: Arasa, "La mansio Ildum de la Via Augusta"

properties.name: Sebelaci
properties.notes: Distances of 24 mp from Ildum and 22 mp to Saguntum are given, but the site itself is not firmly fixed.

properties.name: Saguntum
properties.notes: Famous Iberian/Roman city whose 219 BCE siege triggered the Second Punic War; major node on the coastal road.

properties.name: Valentia
properties.notes: Colonia founded 138 BCE for veterans of the Lusitanian Wars.

properties.name: Sucro
properties.notes: River-mouth station at the Xúquer (ancient Sucro); the river carries the station's own name.

properties.name: Ad Statuas
properties.notes: A modern identification with Oliva appears in Valencian regional scholarship but is not firmly settled.

properties.name: Ad Turres
properties.notes: A genuinely disputed placement on the coastal corridor south of Oliva toward Dénia.

properties.name: Adello
properties.notes: A short 9-mile-pace hop from Ad Turres on the corridor near Calpe/Benissa; no reliable modern fix.

properties.name: Aspis
properties.notes: A name-cognate identification with modern Aspe, inland west of Elche, is suggestive but not archaeologically confirmed.

properties.name: Ilici
properties.notes: Colonia Iulia Ilici Augusta, a major well-excavated colonia near where the Lady of Elche was found.

properties.name: Thiar
properties.notes: A genuinely unidentified station, placed here only as a corridor interpolation between Elche and Cartagena.

properties.name: Carthago Nova
properties.notes: Major Punic-founded port city and capital of the Carthaginensis conventus, with an extensively excavated Roman theatre.

properties.name: Eliocroca
properties.notes: Well-identified inland station on the branch heading toward Baetica.

properties.name: Ad Morum
properties.notes: A tentative identification per regional scholarship on the southern branch of the Via Augusta between Acci and Basti.
sources: AEspA article on the Acci-Basti branch

properties.name: Basti
properties.notes: An important Baetican town on the Guadalquivir-basin approach, well identified archaeologically.

properties.name: Acci
properties.notes: Iulia Gemella Acci, an Augustan veteran colonia and anchor point of the documented southern branch.

properties.name: Acatucci
properties.notes: An obscure station on the mountainous stretch toward Castulo, tentatively placed near Iznalloz.

properties.name: Mentesa Bastia
properties.notes: Distinct from Mentesa Oretana; a genuinely disputed placement near Jódar, Jaén.

properties.name: Castulo
properties.notes: A major pre-Roman and Roman mining town — Hannibal's wife Imilce was said to be from here — and an extensively excavated site.

properties.name: Isturgi
properties.notes: A well-excavated Roman town famous for its terra sigillata pottery kilns, on the north-bank road to Corduba.

properties.name: Epora
properties.notes: On the left bank of the Baetis (Guadalquivir); the modern site preserves the Roman-era name closely.

properties.name: Ad Decumum
properties.notes: A name meaning "at the tenth milestone" from Corduba; placed by distance logic rather than a confirmed site.

properties.name: Corduba
properties.notes: Capital of Hispania Baetica, one of four conventus capitals the Via Augusta is documented to have linked.

properties.name: Ad Aras
properties.notes: A dedicated modern study supports identifying this station with La Carlota, on the Corduba-Astigi stretch.
sources: academic study, "Ad Aras y La Carlota"

properties.name: Astigi
properties.notes: Colonia Augusta Firma Astigi, one of four Baetican conventus capitals, with extensively excavated Roman mosaics.

properties.name: Obucla
properties.notes: A minor town on the direct Astigi-Hispalis road.

properties.name: Carmo
properties.notes: A major hilltop colonia with an exceptionally well-preserved Roman necropolis, on the alternate routing via Hispalis.

properties.name: Hispalis
properties.notes: A major Baetis-river port city and conventus capital.

properties.name: Orippo
properties.notes: A minor station just south of Hispalis on the road to Gades.

properties.name: Ugia
properties.notes: Location debated; placed near Utrera per modern reconstructions.

properties.name: Asta Regia
properties.notes: An important pre-Roman and Roman town near modern Jerez de la Frontera; the archaeological site is well documented.

properties.name: Portus Gaditanus
properties.notes: A port serving Gades across the bay, also cited by Pomponius Mela and the Ravenna Cosmography.

properties.name: Ad Pontem
properties.notes: A name meaning "at the bridge," near the crossing toward the Cadiz peninsula; not firmly fixed.

properties.name: Gades
properties.notes: A Phoenician-founded city (Gadir) and the Via Augusta's southern terminus, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.

properties.name: Hatita
properties.notes: Hatita, at modern Khirbet es-Samra, was a mansio on the Via Traiana Nova between Bostra and Philadelphia, 11 Roman miles along the Peutinger Table's own count. The French School of Jerusalem and the CNRS have studied the site since 1981; a Journal of Roman Archaeology study of the animal bones found here reconstructs what travelers actually ate at a Roman road station.
sources: Journal of Roman Archaeology, "Quid novum ad mensam hodie? The faunal remains from a Roman road station at Khirbet es-Samra, Jordan"

properties.name: Gadda
properties.notes: Gadda sat where modern Zarqa now stands, 13 Roman miles along the Via Traiana Nova from Hatita and 62 more to Philadelphia by the Peutinger Table's count. The Roman camp itself lay southwest of today's bus station and is now built over by the modern city.

properties.name: Thornia
properties.notes: Thornia, known to Ptolemy as Thana and identified today with Tuwaneh in the Wadi al-Hasa, was a substantial mansio roughly 55 hectares in extent, with the Via Traiana Nova itself still traceable running through the wadi below the site. A milestone found here records this stretch of road finished in 110/111 CE, 54 Roman miles north of Petra — one of the freshest, most precisely dated points on the whole road at our 117 CE snapshot.
sources: "Tuwaneh and the Via Nova Traiana in Southern Jordan," Department of Antiquities of Jordan, 1992 season report

properties.name: Rabbathmoba
properties.notes: Rabbathmoba, also called Areopolis, stood at modern Rabba and was one of the region's main towns along the Via Traiana Nova. The Peutinger Table's "Rababatora" likely names this town, though the Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites flags it as possibly a scribal conflation with the separate station of Betthorus further along the road.
sources: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. "Rabbathmoba"

properties.name: Characmoba
properties.notes: Characmoba, recorded by Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE, stood at modern Al-Karak (Kerak) on the Via Traiana Nova's route south from Rabbathmoba, and later became a bishopric under the same name.
sources: Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire, s.v. "Characmoba"

properties.name: Zoara
properties.notes: Zoara, at modern Ghor es-Safi on the southeast shore of the Dead Sea, was folded into the new province of Arabia after 106 CE as a grain-producing station on the Via Traiana Nova. Centuries later the town was still important enough to be named and pictured on the 6th-century Madaba Map mosaic, next to the shrine of Saint Lot.
sources: Madaba Map mosaic, Church of St. George, Madaba

properties.name: Udhruh
properties.notes: Some specialists argue a branch of the Via Traiana Nova bypassed Petra itself, running instead through Udhruh a few kilometers to its east. The monumental legionary fortress visible at Udhruh today is early 4th century, roughly two centuries past this map's 117 CE snapshot — a Trajanic-era road station may have stood here already, but nothing on the scale of the later fort.
sources: Abudanah, Tarawneh, Twaissi, Wenner & Al-Salameen, "The Via Nova Traiana Between Petra and Ayn al-Qana in Arabia Petraea," Oxford Journal of Archaeology 35 (2016), 389-412

properties.name: Zadagatta
properties.notes: Zadagatta, at modern Sadaqa southeast of Petra, sat 18 Roman miles down the Via Traiana Nova by the Peutinger Table's count. David Graf's 1986-89 survey traced two candidate alignments between Petra and Sadaqa and favored the central route through Bir Sarah and Bir Salman as the one that actually matches that distance.
sources: David Graf fieldwork survey 1986-89, summarized in Abudanah et al., Oxford Journal of Archaeology 35 (2016)

properties.name: Hauarra
properties.notes: Hauarra, at modern Humayma, was a major fort-town built around 106-110 CE specifically to guard the newly built Via Traiana Nova — essentially contemporary with this map's 117 CE snapshot. Excavated since 1995 by the Humayma Excavation Project, the site has produced a military bathhouse, a community shrine, a praetorium, a horreum, and a full residential insula.
sources: J.P. Oleson et al., "Preliminary Report of the Humayma Excavation Project 2002, 2004-2005: The Roman Fort"

properties.name: Praesidium
properties.notes: Praesidium, at modern Khirbet al-Khalde in the Wadi al-Yutm, combined a fort with four corner towers, an attached caravanserai, two watchtowers, and the best-preserved Roman-period aqueduct anywhere in the wadi — a genuine waystation for travelers on the last stretch of the Via Traiana Nova into Aila. Named on both the Peutinger Table and the later Notitia Dignitatum, and resurveyed by an international team as recently as 2023.
sources: Harvey, Intagliata & Raja, "Broken glass on the Via Nova Traiana: Roman, Late Antique and Early Islamic activity at Khirbet al-Khalde (south Jordan)," Antiquity

properties.name: Negla
properties.notes: Negla, also called Nejil, stood where modern Shoubak now stands, 22 Roman miles up the Via Traiana Nova from Petra. The site is better known today for its 12th-century Crusader castle, built directly over the older Roman waystation.

properties.name: Betthorus
properties.notes: Betthorus, at modern El-Lejjun, marked a stop on the Via Traiana Nova between Rabbathmoba and Characmoba. The monumental stone legionary fortress visible at the site today, home to the Legio IV Martia, was not built until the late 3rd or early 4th century — close to two centuries after this map's 117 CE snapshot — so nothing on that scale stood here yet at Trajan's death.
sources: S. Thomas Parker, Limes Arabicus Project excavation reports (1980-89)

properties.name: Khirbet al-Kithara
properties.notes: A small Roman military post and watchtower on the Via Traiana Nova between Sadaqa and Humayma. An inscribed milestone found here names both Trajan and Gaius Claudius Severus, the governor who built the road — a direct, dated physical link to the road's own construction.
sources: Livius.org (Jona Lendering), "Khirbet al-Kithara, Milestone mentioning Trajan"

properties.name: Rujm el-Faridiyyeh
properties.notes: A Roman road station on the Via Traiana Nova just south of the Wadi el-Hasa, between Thornia and Rabbathmoba. The physical remains were reportedly bulldozed sometime between 2013 and 2017, but the site's location is well fixed from earlier survey work.

properties.name: Asa Paulini
properties.notes: Asa Paulini stood at modern Anse on the Roman road running north from Lugdunum along the Saone, the first posting station travelers reached leaving the provincial capital. The Antonine Itinerary lists it 15 Roman miles out, and excavation has traced the settlement across roughly 15 hectares beneath and around the modern town, occupied into the 4th century.
sources: Ludna et Asa Paulini, DARA/MOM excavation reports

properties.name: Lunna
properties.notes: Lunna (also transmitted as Ludna) was the second relay north of Lugdunum on the road to Cabillonum, 15 Roman miles beyond Asa Paulini. Modern scholarship splits between Belleville-en-Beaujolais and neighboring Saint-Georges-de-Reneins for the exact spot, so the point marks the identified sector rather than an excavated fix.
sources: Le Patriote Beaujolais, "Lunna, Ludna, Asa Paulini"

properties.name: Matiscone
properties.notes: Matiscone, modern Macon, sat on the Saone 15 Roman miles past Lunna and served as a river-crossing market town on the Lugdunum-Cabillonum road. Roman-era quays and warehouse foundations have been recorded along the modern riverbank.

properties.name: Tinurtium
properties.notes: Tinurtium, identified with Tournus, was a Saone-side mansio 19 Roman miles north of Matiscone. Its river landing kept it busy as a transshipment point for grain and wine barges moving between Lugdunum and the north.

properties.name: Cabillonum
properties.notes: Cabillonum, modern Chalon-sur-Saone, was a major Saone river port 21 Roman miles above Tinurtium and the point where the Via Agrippa network split toward the Rhine frontier. Caesar himself used it as a supply depot during the Gallic War, and its port infrastructure kept growing under Augustus and his successors.

properties.name: Andematunnum
properties.notes: Andematunnum, modern Langres, was the civitas capital of the Lingones and the hinge of the Via Agrippa network, where the road running north from Cabillonum split toward Divodurum and the Rhine and toward Durocortorum and the Channel coast. The Roman town sat on the same defensible plateau the medieval and modern city still occupies.
sources: Voie romaine d'Agrippa, French road-network scholarship

properties.name: Mosa
properties.notes: Mosa, at the hamlet of Meuvy near Andilly-en-Bassigny, was the first relay north of Andematunnum on the road to Divodurum, 12 Roman miles out by the Antonine Itinerary's count.

properties.name: Noviomagus
properties.notes: Noviomagus, modern Nijon, was a small waystation between Mosa and Solimariaca on the Langres-Metz road. The Tabula Peutingeriana places it 7 Gallic leagues from Solimariaca; the surviving Antonine Itinerary text does not give its own mile figure from Mosa.

properties.name: Solimariaca
properties.notes: Solimariaca, identified with Soulosse-sous-Saint-Elophe, was a substantial roadside settlement 16 Roman miles from Mosa, built around a Gallo-Roman sanctuary complex that draws its own excavation literature separate from the road station itself.

properties.name: Tullum
properties.notes: Tullum, modern Toul, was the civitas capital of the Leuci, 15 Roman miles past Solimariaca on the road to Divodurum. It kept its walled Roman street grid legible enough that the medieval and modern town still traces it in part.

properties.name: Scarponna
properties.notes: Scarponna, at modern Dieulouard on the Moselle, was the last relay before Divodurum, roughly 15 Roman miles from Tullum by the Peutinger Table's count. The straight Roman alignment between Toul and Dieulouard is still traceable on the ground today, passing the Libdeau farm and a former Roman camp near Rosieres-en-Haye.

properties.name: Divodurum
properties.notes: Divodurum, modern Metz, was the civitas capital of the Mediomatrici and the central hub of the Via Agrippa network in eastern Gaul, where roads converged toward Augusta Treverorum, Durocortorum, Mogontiacum, and Argentorate. Its amphitheatre, one of the largest in Gaul, could seat an estimated 25,000 spectators.

properties.name: Caranusca
properties.notes: Caranusca, tentatively placed at Hettange-Grande near Thionville, was a station on the more direct left-bank branch of the Metz-Trier road, 42 Roman miles out by the Tabula Peutingeriana's figure. Early 20th-century Luxembourgish scholarship debated the exact spot, with an alternate proposal at Garche.

properties.name: Ricciacum
properties.notes: Ricciacum, at modern Dalheim in Luxembourg, was a large Gallo-Roman vicus on the Metz-Trier road, 10 Roman miles from Caranusca and another 10 short of Augusta Treverorum. Excavations have uncovered a forum, temples, and a theatre built to seat roughly 3,500 people, among the best-preserved secondary settlements on the whole road.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre at Dalheim (Ricciacum), Luxembourg · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ibliodurum
properties.notes: Ibliodurum was the first relay west of Divodurum on the road to Durocortorum, 8 Roman miles out. Its exact location is disputed among archaeologists working the Woevre plain; a station near Vionville, on the line of an old road above the Iron river, is one candidate.
sources: Revue archeologique de l'Est 61 (2012), "Vionville: station routiere d'Ibliodurum?"

properties.name: Fines
properties.notes: Fines, whose name simply means "the boundary," was a mutatio 6 Roman miles from Ibliodurum, likely marking a tribal border crossed by the Reims-Metz road. French rescue archaeology places it somewhere between Haudiomont, Manheulles, and the deserted village of Aulnois, without a firm fix.
sources: Revue archeologique de l'Est 61 (2012), "Manheulles: la station routiere antique de Fines?"

properties.name: Virodunum
properties.notes: Virodunum, modern Verdun, was a fortified river town on the Meuse 9 Roman miles from Fines, controlling the crossing on the Reims-Metz road. It kept this strategic role for the rest of antiquity, walled again as a late Roman castrum.

properties.name: Axuena
properties.notes: Axuena was a relay 17 Roman miles from Virodunum on the road toward Durocortorum, in the Argonne forest corridor the modern road still follows. No modern village has been confidently matched to it, so the point is set by interpolation along the attested road line.

properties.name: Basilia
properties.notes: Basilia was the last relay before Durocortorum, 12 Roman miles out, on the Reims-Metz road through the Argonne. Like its neighbor Axuena, no secure modern identification has stuck, and the point here is interpolated along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Durocortorum
properties.notes: Durocortorum, modern Reims, was the civitas capital of the Remi and one of the largest cities in Gaul, sitting at the junction of the Via Agrippa branch to Divodurum and the road running northwest to Bagacum and the Channel. Its forum's underground gallery, the cryptoportique, still survives beneath the modern Place du Forum.

properties.name: Duronum
properties.notes: Duronum, recorded locally as "Strata Duronum," was the first stage out of Durocortorum on the road to Bagacum, 12 Roman miles along. It is identified with modern Etroeungt in the Avesnois, where the old road name survived in local toponymy.

properties.name: Verbinum
properties.notes: Verbinum (Vironum on the Antonine Itinerary), modern Vervins, sat 10 Roman miles from Duronum at the junction of the Reims-Bavay road and a secondary route toward Saint-Quentin, on the edge of Viromanduan territory.

properties.name: Catusiacum
properties.notes: Catusiacum was a short 6-mile hop from Verbinum, placed by local archaeology just north of the village of Chaourse in the Aisne valley.

properties.name: Minatiacum
properties.notes: Minatiacum, called Ninittaci on the Tabula Peutingeriana, is identified with modern Nizy-le-Comte, 7 Roman miles from Catusiacum on the road north to Bagacum.

properties.name: Muenna
properties.notes: Muenna was the last relay before Bagacum, 8 Roman miles out, but no modern village has been convincingly matched to the name. The point is interpolated along the Vervins-Bavay road corridor between its known neighbors.

properties.name: Bagacum
properties.notes: Bagacum, modern Bavay, was the civitas capital of the Nervii and the busiest road junction in northern Gaul, where seven roads met including the routes to Durocortorum, Gesoriacum, Colonia Agrippina, and Samarobriva. Its excavated forum complex, over 2.5 hectares with walls still standing more than 10 meters high in places, is among the largest Roman civic sites uncovered in France.
properties.image_credit: Forum antique de Bavay (Bagacum) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pons Scaldis
properties.notes: Pons Scaldis, "the Scheldt bridge," marked the river crossing on the Bavay-Tournai road at modern Escautpont, 12 Roman miles from Bagacum. The name survives almost unchanged in the modern town's own.

properties.name: Turnacum
properties.notes: Turnacum, modern Tournai, was a civitas capital of the Menapii and a river port on the Scheldt, 12 Roman miles from the Pons Scaldis crossing. It later became a Merovingian royal seat, but its Roman-era street grid and cemeteries are extensively documented.

properties.name: Viroviacum
properties.notes: Viroviacum, identified with Wervik on the Lys, was a relay 16 Roman miles from Turnacum on the road toward the Channel coast.

properties.name: Castellum Menapiorum
properties.notes: Castellum Menapiorum, modern Cassel, stood on a striking hilltop in the flat Flanders plain, 16 Roman miles from Viroviacum, and controlled roads radiating toward Boulogne, Therouanne, Arras, and Wervik. Decades of rescue excavation there have uncovered a dense street grid, temples, and a small amphitheatre.

properties.name: Tarvenna
properties.notes: Tarvenna, modern Therouanne, was the civitas capital of the Morini, 9 Roman miles from Castellum Menapiorum on the final stretch to Gesoriacum. It later grew into a major medieval bishopric before Charles V's forces razed it in 1553, which is why so little of the ancient or medieval town survives above ground today.

properties.name: Gesoriacum
properties.notes: Gesoriacum, modern Boulogne-sur-Mer, was the main crossing point to Britannia and home port of the Classis Britannica, the fleet Claudius based there for his 43 CE invasion. A lighthouse, later remembered as the Tour d'Ordre and sometimes credited to Caligula, stood over the harbor until it finally collapsed in 1644.

properties.name: Forum Segusiavorum
properties.notes: Forum Segusiavorum, modern Feurs, was the market and administrative center of the Segusiavi and the first major stage on Agrippa's road out of Lugdunum, roughly 50 km away as the crow flies. The Peutinger Table marks the start of its Gallic-league distance convention right at this stretch, noting 'usque hic legas' beside Lyon's own label. It remained the civitas capital of the Segusiavi from the late 1st century BCE into the 3rd century CE.

properties.name: Rodumna
properties.notes: Rodumna was a Segusiavan river-crossing town on the Loire, named by Ptolemy and marked as Roidomna on the Peutinger Table on the road between Forum Segusiavorum and Augustonemetum. Roanne functioned as a crossroads linking Lyon, Feurs, Vichy, Clermont-Ferrand, and the Arroux valley, and the settlement's disputed intermediate station 'Mediolanum' may have split this stretch, a debate the Peutinger Table's own conflicting readings haven't settled.
sources: Genin & Lavendhomme, 'Rodumna (Roanne, Loire), le village gallo-romain'

properties.name: Ariolica
properties.notes: Ariolica appears on the Peutinger Table on the road between Rodumna and Vorogium, but its modern site is unsettled. Local antiquarian tradition places it at La Pacaudiere, while a Peutinger-based topographic reconstruction favors Artaix, on the ancient Loire-valley road linking Roanne to Digoin. The station's existence and position on this itinerary are firm; only its precise footprint is disputed.

properties.name: Vorogium
properties.notes: Vorogium sat on the Allier per the Peutinger Table, on the road toward the thermal station of Aquis Calidis. It is identified with modern Varennes-sur-Allier, recorded locally as Vorocium at the hamlet of Vouroux. The station lay on the direct road linking Rodumna to Augustonemetum through the Bourbonnais.

properties.name: Aquis Calidis
properties.notes: Aquis Calidis, 'at the warm waters,' names the thermal springs of Vichy and sat on the Peutinger Table's road toward Augustonemetum. Earlier scholars floated rival identifications at Saint-Maurice or Mont-Dore, but the genuine hot springs and proven Gallo-Roman occupation at Vichy settled the identification. The Peutinger Table marks the site with its standard thermal-establishment symbol.
sources: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, 'Aquae Calidae (Vichy)'

properties.name: Augustonemetum
properties.notes: Augustonemetum was the Augustan-era civitas capital of the Arverni and the central hub of Agrippa's road toward Aquitania, sitting between Lugdunum and Augustoritum. It now lies beneath modern Clermont-Ferrand, whose Gallo-Roman remains are catalogued in a dedicated topographic atlas.

properties.name: Ubrilium
properties.notes: Ubrilium was the first cursus publicus stop west of Augustonemetum on Agrippa's road. Its modern site is contested: Pierre Denimal argued for Mazaye, Frederic Trement proposed the excavated Gallo-Roman settlement at the Col de Ceyssat below Puy de Dome, and Pierre-Francois Fournier favored Olby. All three candidates sit within a few kilometers of each other on the same westward corridor.

properties.name: Acitodunum
properties.notes: Acitodunum was a mutatio of the Lugdunum-Mediolanum Santonum road, sited at modern Ahun in the Creuse, within the civitas of the Lemovices. It appears by name on the Peutinger Table, though its exact distance from the previous station is disputed among the sources checked. Ahun continued as a significant Gallo-Roman vicus into Late Antiquity, with an associated necropolis nearby at Pontarion.

properties.name: Augustoritum
properties.notes: Augustoritum was the Augustan civitas capital of the Lemovices and the last major hub before Agrippa's road descended into the Charente valley toward Cassinomagus and Saintes. Excavations under modern Limoges have traced its street grid and public buildings.

properties.name: Cassinomagus
properties.notes: Cassinomagus was a 130-hectare secondary agglomeration on the western edge of Lemovices territory, famous today for the exceptionally well-preserved two-story Gallo-Roman baths known as the Thermes de Longeas. Jacques Dassie's corrected reading of the Peutinger Table places it on the road from Augustoritum toward Mediolanum Santonum. The site anchors the modern Cassinomagus archaeological park at Chassenon, Charente.
sources: Peutinger Table, corrected reading per J. Dassie (archaero.com)

properties.name: Sermanicomagus
properties.notes: Sermanicomagus, likely a scribal corruption of Germanicomagus, sat on the road from Cassinomagus to Mediolanum Santonum per the Peutinger Table. Aerial archaeologist Jacques Dassie locates it at La Terne, a hamlet of Luxe with Gallo-Roman paving and villa remains, while the 19th-century Abbe Michon argued for Charme based on nearby villa remains, though the known road alignment runs well south of Charme. The station is real and firmly on this itinerary; only its precise modern footprint is unresolved.
sources: J. Dassie, Peutinger Table reading for this road (archaero.com)

properties.name: Aunedonnacum
properties.notes: Aunedonnacum was a secondary Gallo-Roman agglomeration at modern Aulnay-de-Saintonge, on the Peutinger Table's road toward Mediolanum Santonum. The Antonine Itinerary's Bordeaux route classifies settlements of this kind among its vici, distinct from full civitas capitals. The site sits at a crossing of routes linking Poitiers, Saintes, and the Limousin.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana, per J. Dassie's corrected reading

properties.name: Mediolanum Santonum
properties.notes: Mediolanum Santonum was the civitas capital of the Santones and the western anchor of Agrippa's road, standing past Aunedonnacum in the Peutinger Table's corrected reading. The town gives its name to the modern reconstruction 'Voie romaine d'Agrippa (Saintes-Lyon),' formally numbered VR 27 between Saintes and Limoges in the 19th-century K. Miller classification of French Roman roads. From here the same road network continues southwest via the Antonine Itinerary toward Novioregum and Burdigala.

properties.name: Novioregum
properties.notes: Novioregum was a Gallo-Roman port town on the Gironde estuary linking Mediolanum Santonum southward to Tamnum, Blavia, and Burdigala. The Antonine Itinerary places it on this stretch, an identification resting on substantial Gallo-Roman remains excavated at Barzan, between Talmont-sur-Gironde and Arces-sur-Gironde.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini, iter a Burdigala Mediolanum Santonum

properties.name: Tamnum
properties.notes: Tamnum was a waystation on the Burdigala-Mediolanum Santonum road, conventionally identified with modern Consac in Charente-Maritime. Its coordinates here mark the commune center, since no precise archaeological footprint for the ancient station itself turned up in the sources checked. It sat on the road corridor connecting Saintes to Blaye and Bordeaux.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini, iter a Burdigala Mediolanum Santonum

properties.name: Blavia
properties.notes: Blavia guarded a Gironde estuary crossing on the Antonine Itinerary's road linking Bordeaux to Saintes, south of Tamnum. The identification with modern Blaye is secure, resting on continuous toponymic descent from Blavia to Blaye. In Late Antiquity the site was refortified as one of the castella listed in the Notitia Galliarum.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini, iter a Burdigala Mediolanum Santonum

properties.name: Vienna
properties.notes: Vienna, modern Vienne, stood 23 Roman miles south of Lugdunum on the Antonine Itinerary's Rhone route and was the first major stage on the Narbonensis branch of the Via Agrippa. The road split here into two alternate courses toward Valentia, one along each bank of the Rhone, with the Itinerary recording a longer 23-mile stage and a shorter 16-mile alternative. Vienna served as the civitas capital of the Allobroges and anchored the road's southern departure point from Lugdunum's network.

properties.name: Figlinis
properties.notes: Figlinis marked the Antonine Itinerary's next stop 17 Roman miles south of Vienna. Scholars place the station at Saint-Rambert-d'Albon on the Rhone's left bank, a reading cross-checked against the original Peutinger Table. It functioned as a horse-changing point on the road linking Vienna to Valentia.
sources: Vienne dans les textes grecs et latins, MOM Editions, books.openedition.org/momeditions/1014

properties.name: Ursolis
properties.notes: Ursolis, also spelled Ursinis, appeared in the Antonine Itinerary between Figlinis and Tegna on the Vienna-Valentia stretch, cited at 26 Roman miles south of Vienna and 22 miles north of Valentia. Its modern site is disputed: a Peutinger Table-based reading places it at Saint-Vallier-sur-Rhone, while an older etymological argument instead proposed Roussillon. The station is genuinely attested in the itinerary text; only its precise findspot remains unresolved.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Valentia-Ursolis 22 m.p.; Ursolis-Vienna 26 m.p., cumulative)
Les stations routieres dans la cite de Vienne, Revue archeologique de Narbonnaise 38 (2005), persee.fr

properties.name: Tegna
properties.notes: Tegna sat on the Via Agrippa at modern Tain-l'Hermitage, 8 Roman miles north of Valentia according to the Antonine Itinerary's cumulative mile-count. Excavations there uncovered a temple, a taurobolium altar, a tower, and the remains of substantial dwellings, marking it as a real roadside settlement rather than a bare relay post. It depended administratively on the colony of Vienna.

properties.name: Valentia
properties.notes: Valentia, modern Valence, was recorded as a civitas stop on the Via Agrippa in both the Antonine Itinerary and the 333 CE Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary, 8 Roman miles south of Tegna. A milestone dedicated to Antoninus Pius, found in the park of La Paillasse near Etoile-sur-Rhone, marked the sixth Roman mile south of the town and confirms the road's course out of Valentia toward Arausio.
sources: Voie romaine d'Agrippa, fr.wikipedia.org (Antoninus Pius milestone, Etoile-sur-Rhone)

properties.name: Umbenno
properties.notes: Umbenno was a horse-changing station the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary placed 9 Roman miles south of Valentia. French archaeologists locate it at Les Battendons in the commune of Etoile-sur-Rhone, close to where the Antoninus Pius milestone marking the sixth Roman mile from Valence was found. It served travelers on the Via Agrippa's stretch down the Rhone's left bank toward Acunum.

properties.name: Bantiana
properties.notes: Bantiana, also written Batiana, was a relay station cited in both the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary and the Peutinger Table, set 12 Roman miles south of Umbenno. It stood near modern Saulce-sur-Rhone, where the toponym Bance still survives and where pottery and brick fragments have turned up in the fields. No structural remains of the road itself survive at the site today.

properties.name: Acunum
properties.notes: Acunum, modern Montelimar, was the only stop between Valentia and Arausio that the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary classed as a full mansio rather than a simple mutatio, reached 12 Roman miles south of Bantiana. The Roman settlement grew a forum, aqueducts, and baths at the confluence of the Roubion and the Rhone.
sources: Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire, Akousion/Acunum, dare.ht.lu.se

properties.name: Novem Craris
properties.notes: Novem Craris was a change-station the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary placed 10 Roman miles south of Acunum, at the point where the Via Agrippa crossed the Berre stream. French scholars locate it at Le Logis de Berre in the commune of Les Granges-Gontardes, one of the minor relay posts on the Tricastin stretch of the road toward Arausio.

properties.name: Ad Letoce
properties.notes: Ad Letoce, also called Senomagos in some sources, was a relay station the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary set 10 Roman miles south of Novem Craris, at the crossing of the Lez river. Researchers identify the site with Saint-Pierre-de-Senos in the commune of Bollene, one of the last stops before reaching the civitas of Arausio.
sources: Le Tricastin romain: evolution d'un paysage centurie, Alpara/OpenEdition, books.openedition.org/alpara/2835

properties.name: Arausio
properties.notes: Arausio, modern Orange, was recorded as a civitas stop on the Via Agrippa in the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary, reached 13 Roman miles south of Ad Letoce. This entry pins it specifically as a mile-marked itinerary station on Agrippa's Rhone road rather than as a general Roman city entry. Nine Roman milestones have been found along the stretch of road between Valentia and Arausio, the earliest dedicated to Tiberius.

properties.name: Cypresseta
properties.notes: Cypresseta was a change-station the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary placed 15 Roman miles south of Arausio, on the road's approach to Avenione. Local tradition situates it near La Traille in the commune of Sorgues, though the identification is less firmly fixed than its neighboring stations.

properties.name: Avenione
properties.notes: Avenione, modern Avignon, appeared as a civitas stop on the Via Agrippa in the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary, 5 Roman miles south of Cypresseta. This entry pins Avignon specifically as a mile-marked Via Agrippa station rather than describing its later medieval fame. The road continued south from here toward Ernaginum, where it joined the Via Domitia.

properties.name: Ernaginum
properties.notes: Ernaginum, identified with the Saint-Gabriel chapel site in the commune of Tarascon, was the change-station where the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary placed the Via Agrippa's junction with the Via Domitia, south of Avenione and short of Arelate. No bridge crossed the Rhone downstream of Lugdunum in this period, so traffic bound for Arelate or west toward Nemausus and Narbo Martius funneled through this junction by road and ferry.

properties.name: Ad Rubras (Saxa Rubra)
properties.notes: Ad Rubras stood nine Roman miles north of Rome on the Via Flaminia, at the point where the Via Tiberina split off toward the river valley. The station took its name from the reddish volcanic outcrops (saxa rubra) along the road and later lent its name to the nearby site of Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE. The Tabula Peutingeriana marks it among the first stops leaving the city.

properties.name: Ad Vicesimum
properties.notes: Ad Vicesimum marked the twentieth Roman mile of the Via Flaminia, named simply for its milepost like many roadside changing-stations. The Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary of 333 CE records it eleven miles beyond Ad Rubras and twelve short of Aqua Viva. Its exact site in the Tiber valley north of Rome, somewhere near modern Castelnuovo di Porto or Morlupo, has never been pinpointed archaeologically.

properties.name: Rostrata Villa
properties.notes: Rostrata Villa appeared in the Antonine Itinerary as a stage twenty-four miles from Rome, likely named for a villa decorated with ship's-beak (rostra) trophies. Gazetteers place it in the territory of Rignano Flaminio, though no excavation has fixed the exact site on the ground. It sat on the stretch of road running through the Tiber valley toward Civita Castellana.

properties.name: Aqua Viva
properties.notes: Aqua Viva was a horse-changing mutatio recorded by the Bordeaux Pilgrim and marked on the Tabula Peutingeriana between Ad Vicesimum and Ocriculum. Its name, 'living water,' points to a spring or perennial stream that supplied travelers, a common naming pattern for Roman roadside halts. Its precise findspot in the hills near Civita Castellana has not been confirmed by excavation.

properties.name: Ocriculum
properties.notes: Ocriculum stood forty-four Roman miles from Rome where the Flaminia ran close along the east bank of the Tiber, the first Umbrian town travelers reached heading north. The archaeological park below modern Otricoli has exposed its forum, theater, amphitheater, baths, and a stretch of the paved road itself. Both the Antonine Itinerary and the Bordeaux Pilgrim list it as a civitas stop.

properties.name: Narnia
properties.notes: Narnia occupied a defensible spur above the Nera gorge, reached by the Bridge of Augustus, and had been a Latin colony since 299 BCE, long before the road reached it. The town was where the Flaminia split into two branches to Forum Flaminii: one via Interamna and Spoletium, the other via Carsulae and Mevania. The Antonine Itinerary places it fifty-six Roman miles from Rome.

properties.name: Interamna Nahars
properties.notes: Interamna Nahars, 'between the rivers' for its position among branches of the Nera, lay on the eastern branch of the Flaminia that the Antonine Itinerary and the Bordeaux Pilgrim record instead of the more direct route via Carsulae. This loop was already in regular use by the later first century CE and added roughly a dozen miles to the trip to Forum Flaminii. Modern Terni preserves the ancient street grid inside its historic center.

properties.name: Spoletium
properties.notes: Spoletium was a Latin colony founded in 241 BCE that the eastern branch of the Flaminia later folded into its route between Interamna and Forum Flaminii. Its Roman theater, amphitheater, and the Ponte Sanguinario still stand beneath the medieval town. The Antonine Itinerary places it eighteen miles beyond Interamna on the branch line.
sources: Itin. Ant. 83 m.p. ab Urbe (Interamna branch)

properties.name: Forum Flaminii
properties.notes: Forum Flaminii owed its founding to Gaius Flaminius himself, planted as a market vicus where the road's two branches reunited before climbing into the Apennines. The Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary places it twenty miles beyond Spoletium; the Antonine Itinerary gives a slightly shorter eighteen, a routine discrepancy between the surviving sources. The site survives as the frazione of San Giovanni Profiamma outside Foligno, where a Roman arch still spans the old road.
sources: Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, civitas Foro Flaminii ~20 m.p. post Spoletium

properties.name: Nuceria Camellaria
properties.notes: Nuceria Camellaria took its epithet from the camellaria, pack-mule stables serving traffic bound for the Apennine passes. The Tabula Peutingeriana and the Bordeaux Pilgrim both place it twelve miles beyond Forum Flaminii, though the surviving Antonine Itinerary text skips straight from Forum Flaminii to Helvillum without naming it. Modern Nocera Umbra continues the ancient name on the same spur above the road.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana; Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, 12 m.p. post Forum Flaminii

properties.name: Tadinum
properties.notes: Tadinum stood in the plain below the hill where medieval Gualdo Tadino later grew, on the stretch of the Flaminia a few miles short of Helvillum. Rome took the Umbrian settlement in 266 BCE, well before Flaminius built the road past it, and the town later gave its name to the decisive Battle of Taginae in 552 CE.
sources: Itinerarium Burdigalense, civitas Tadinum (derived split from Nuceria)

properties.name: Helvillum
properties.notes: Helvillum appears in all four surviving Roman itineraries of the Via Flaminia, making it one of the best-attested mutationes on the mountain stretch of the road, yet its exact site is disputed. Most scholars place it at Sigillo, though some argue for neighboring Fossato di Vico instead, since no inscription has fixed the station on the ground. The Antonine Itinerary places it 128 Roman miles from Rome, just before the climb to the Scheggia pass.

properties.name: Ad Ensem
properties.notes: Ad Ensem sat at the Passo della Scheggia, 632 meters up, where the Via Flaminia crossed the main Apennine ridge and left Umbria for the ager Gallicus. The Tabula Peutingeriana and the Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary both record a mutatio here between Helvillum and Cales. The frazione of Scheggia still sits just below the pass on the modern SS3.
sources: Itinerarium Burdigalense (route via Ad Ensem/Scheggia Pass)

properties.name: Luceoli
properties.notes: Luceoli grew as a vicus where the road descended from the Scheggia pass into the Cantiano valley, and later became a Byzantine-era diocese in its own right. A Roman milestone found at Cantiano and dated 305 CE recorded the site as the 140th mile from Rome, and the nearby frazione of Pontericcioli still preserves the name through 'Pons Luceoli.' It appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana between the Apennine crossing and Cales.
sources: CIL milestone, Cantiano, mile CXL (dated 305 CE)

properties.name: Cales (Ad Calem)
properties.notes: Cales, 'Ad Calem' in the itineraries, was the eighth principal stage the Antonine Itinerary lists on the Via Flaminia, set on a hill between the Bosso and Burano streams. Cagli's archaeological museum displays finds from the Roman settlement, whose checkerboard street plan still shows through the medieval town above it. The Antonine Itinerary fixes it 151 Roman miles from Rome.

properties.name: Intercisa
properties.notes: Intercisa, 'the cut-through,' named the narrow gorge of the Candigliano river that the Flaminia crossed by tunnel, first bored in the third century BCE and enlarged by Vespasian in 76-77 CE, a work his own dedicatory inscription at the site still records. The Jerusalem Itinerary and the Tabula Peutingeriana both list the mutatio here, nine Roman miles short of Forum Sempronii. The tunnel remains walkable today inside the Passo del Furlo nature reserve.
sources: Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum; Tabula Peutingeriana, mutatio Ad Intercisa, 9 m.p. a Foro Sempronii

properties.name: Forum Sempronii
properties.notes: Forum Sempronii marked the point where the Via Flaminia emerged from the Apennine gorges into the Metauro valley, a market town the Antonine Itinerary places 169 Roman miles from Rome. Excavations at modern Fossombrone have uncovered its forum, an amphitheater, and stretches of the ancient road surface. The site controlled traffic funneling out of the Furlo pass toward the Adriatic coast.

properties.name: Fanum Fortunae
properties.notes: Fanum Fortunae, named for a temple to Fortuna near the road, was where the Via Flaminia finally reached the Adriatic after crossing the Apennines. Augustus refounded it as the colonia Iulia Fanestris and built the three-arched Arco d'Augusto that still stands as the town gate where the Flaminia entered the walls. Itinerary sources place it roughly 185 miles from Rome overall.

properties.name: Pisaurum
properties.notes: Pisaurum was founded as a Roman colony in 184 BCE, decades before the Via Flaminia reached it, and grew into the last major stop before the road's terminus at Ariminum. The Antonine Itinerary records it 193 Roman miles from Rome and eight beyond Fanum Fortunae. Modern Pesaro's historic center overlies the Roman street grid at the mouth of the Foglia river.

properties.name: Ad Compitum
properties.notes: Ad Compitum served as a horse-changing station on the Via Aemilia, its name simply meaning 'at the crossroads.' The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it as the first stop the Bordeaux pilgrim passed after leaving Ariminum in 333 CE, on the stretch running toward Caesena. No archaeological remains have been tied definitively to the site, and its precise location along the corridor east of Cesena remains unconfirmed.

properties.name: Caesena
properties.notes: Caesena stood on the Via Aemilia as a river town on the Savio, appearing in the Antonine Itinerary as 'Curva Caesena' twenty Roman miles out of Ariminum. Julius Caesar named it alongside Ariminum during his march on Rome in 49 BCE, and the Itinerarium Burdigalense listed it as a civitas six miles beyond the mutatio Ad Compitum. Modern Cesena's historic center preserves the Roman street grid along the line of the ancient road.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam (Curva Caesena)

properties.name: Forum Popilii
properties.notes: Forum Popilii took its name from the consul Publius Popillius Laenas, credited with founding the town around 132 BCE. Pliny the Elder listed it among the municipia of Gallia Cispadana, and both the Tabula Peutingeriana and the Itinerarium Burdigalense placed it on the Via Aemilia between Caesena and Forum Livii. Modern Forlimpopoli sits on the Roman site, roughly midway between Cesena and Forli.

properties.name: Forum Livii
properties.notes: Forum Livii arose as a forum along the Via Aemilia, most likely named for the censor Marcus Livius Salinator in the early second century BCE. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it as a civitas five miles beyond Forum Popilii, and the Antonine Itinerary placed the combined stretch from Caesena at thirteen miles. Modern Forli grew directly from the Roman settlement, retaining its position astride the ancient road.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Faventia
properties.notes: Faventia sat on the Via Aemilia between Forum Livii and Forum Cornelii, a colonia by the late Republic and the site of a decisive Social War battle in 82 BCE. The Antonine Itinerary placed it ten Roman miles from Forum Livii, and the Itinerarium Burdigalense listed it as a civitas on the same stretch. Modern Faenza occupies the ancient site, later famous for the maiolica pottery that gave faience its name.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Forum Cornelii
properties.notes: Forum Cornelii was founded as a forum along the Via Aemilia, traditionally linked to Lucius Cornelius Sulla, who resettled veterans there after 82 BCE. The Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerarium Burdigalense both listed it as a civitas on the stretch running toward Claterna. Modern Imola preserves the Roman decumanus as its main street, with the ancient forum beneath the historic center.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Claterna
properties.notes: Claterna grew from a Via Aemilia waypoint into a town comparable in size to its neighbors Bononia and Forum Cornelii, founded in the first half of the second century BCE. The Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerarium Burdigalense both recorded it as a civitas on the stretch between Forum Cornelii and Bononia. Excavations at Ozzano dell'Emilia have uncovered its forum, theater, amphitheater, and a stretch of the paved road, now an archaeological park.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Bononia
properties.notes: Bononia was recorded as a fixed civitas waypoint on the Via Aemilia's own itinerary listing, ten Roman miles beyond Claterna by both the Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerarium Burdigalense. Both sources used it as the point where the road from Ariminum met the routes climbing south into the Apennines. The Bordeaux pilgrim's 333 CE account measured the onward stretch toward Mutina from this point.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Ad Medias
properties.notes: Ad Medias, 'the middle station,' served as a horse-changing point on the Via Aemilia at roughly the center of the long, straight run between Bononia and Mutina. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it fifteen Roman miles out of Bononia on the pilgrim's route in 333 CE. Its exact location, likely near modern Castelfranco Emilia or Bazzano, has not been fixed by excavation.

properties.name: Victoriola
properties.notes: Victoriola functioned as a mutatio on the Via Aemilia between Ad Medias and Mutina, its diminutive name meaning 'little victory.'
